tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content: markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema. Use it when the request identifies a page and needs its content or defined fields. Use `firecrawl_search` when additional web sources are needed; on an authenticated session, `firecrawl_map` lists a site's URLs and `firecrawl_crawl` collects a set of pages.

Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch or a smaller `maxAge` to bound staleness. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled. Authenticated responses can include a `metadata.scrapeId` for optional scrape feedback.

On an authenticated session with Alexandria access, `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching provider returns typed records in one call. Keyless sessions have no provider matches.

Alexandria mode, on an authenticated session with Alexandria access: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. tools.name: mcp__mcphub-automation__firecrawl-firecrawl_search
tools.description:
Search web, news, or image sources and return ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description; use `firecrawl_scrape` on a result URL when the excerpt is not enough.

Authenticated search also returns matching Alexandria data providers in data.tools (companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more). Prefer a provider over scraping pages when the task needs the same fields across several entities, exact figures or timestamps, provenance, or many records; use web results when they already answer the question. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false.

On an authenticated session, tool matches describe available capabilities; `firecrawl_find_tools` returns their contracts and `firecrawl_scrape` with an `alexandria` body executes a selected capability. Keyless sessions get no Alexandria matches in data.tools.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`; its hits return in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; authenticated sessions also have `firecrawl_gov_search` as the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. `categories: ["research"]` restricts web results to research-affiliated websites; the `firecrawl_research_*` tools are a separate surface over paper abstracts and full text (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv). Query operators, domain filters, `categories`, `toolDetail` and `scrapeOptions` are described on their parameters. Returns source-type result groups and usage metadata. Authenticated responses can include an `id` for optional search feedback.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

scrapeOptions.description: Attach page content for web results in the same call. These fetches ignore maxAge, so use firecrawl_scrape when you need a live fetch. scrapeOptions fetches web pages, never Alexandria provider tools.

content.text:
A subagent is now fixing those 9 findings in the batch 0 worktree, adding one new commit on top of `8700a9ab`. Each fix comes with a harness test that has to fail without the fix. I'll check the result against the full suite, coverage and `prek`, then run the second and final review round before opening the test-only PR.

Batch 0 also found a new open bug: if a lock's writes fail as "disconnected" while its reads succeed, the slot never suspends. Every successful read resets the lock breaker, so the slot retries every 2 seconds forever. I've added it to the catalog for an expected-failure test in batch 11.

I also corrected the memory note about pytest-timeout. It didn't stop a busy loop on a frozen clock, but it did stop a teardown stuck waiting on a call, so neither outcome is reliable.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Three of the findings share one root: the harness answered "did this ever happen?" when the test needed "is this happening now?" `async_wait_held` asked whether a call was ever held, not whether one is held now. `clear_faults` released only the faults still listed, not every fault that was installed. `ignore` counted calls that could never have been ignored. A regression test built on that kind of check passes without testing anything.
- Finding 6 matters most for the rebuild: jumping the clock 2 s at once fires every timer due in that window together. A test can then see a race that can't happen in production, or miss one that can. Stepping to each timer's due time in turn keeps them in the same order production would.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

content.text:
I'd revert nothing, with one exception: `#1629` introduced a regression that needs a small fix before 6.0.2 is published. Waiting for the refactor won't cover it, because the refactor is paused.

**Why not revert the rest:**
- **The fixes hold up.** Nothing we've found shows any merged fix to be wrong. Reverting them would bring back bugs that users reported.
- **The provider fixes are permanent anyway.** `#1624`, `#1625` and `#1627` sit in the provider layer, which a core rebuild keeps.
- **The core fixes pass their behavior to the new code.** `#1623`, `#1629`, `#1632` and `#1633` live in the code a rebuild would replace. Batch 1 turns their tests into checks on entity state that fail when the fix is removed. So what they fixed becomes the spec the new core has to meet, and their code goes away with the old core. That part does take care of itself.
- **`#1634` is behavior-neutral.** The rebuild either reuses its predicate names or deletes them, and reverting now would just be churn.

**The exception:** since `#1629`, the shared lock coordinator has no config entry. As a result, a user's "Disable polling" setting is now ignored for every lock. I logged this in the regression catalog as OPEN, to be fixed in R2. R2 is now paused behind the regression net, though, and 6.0.2 is a draft that already includes `#1629`. Publishing it as-is would ship the regression.

You already approved the rule: poll unless every entry using the lock has disabled polling (decision 2). It's a small fix on its own:
- Override the coordinator's refresh scheduling to check the entries that hold the lock.
- Add one test that drives entity state and fails when the fix is removed.

That doesn't need any of R2's lock-handle work. I'd make it a one-defect PR from main now, in parallel with the batch 0 fixes, and publish 6.0.2 once it merges.

One open question: the R2-0 review found that a failed setup leaves a state listener running. I don't know whether `#1629` caused that or it was already there. Batch 3 will check it with a test, and if `#1629` caused it, it gets the same kind of quick fix.

class LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator(
    DataUpdateCoordinator[dict[CredentialAddress, SlotCredential]]
):
    """Class to manage usercode updates."""

    def __init__(self, hass: HomeAssistant, lock: BaseLock) -> None:
        """Initialize the usercode update coordinator."""
        self._lock = lock
        self._drift_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        self._connection_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        # Disable periodic polling when push updates are supported.
        # Polling is still used for initial load.
        #
        # A bridged provider may not know the answer yet: it derives push
        # support from discovery data that arrives on the broker's schedule,
        # so a lock constructed before that lands looks like a poll lock.
        # ``note_push_capability`` is the one place that answer is revisited.
        self._is_push = lock.supports_push
        update_interval = None if self._is_push else lock.usercode_scan_interval
        super().__init__(
            hass,
            _LOGGER,
            name=f"{DOMAIN} {lock.lock.entity_id}",
            update_method=self.async_get_usercodes,
            update_interval=update_interval,
            # Belongs to the lock, which several entries can share, not to any
            # one of them: Lock Code Manager shuts it down once the last entry
            # holding the lock lets go (``async_unload_lock``). The "Disable
            # polling" system option, which Home Assistant reads from a
            # coordinator's own entry, therefore does not apply.
            config_entry=None,
        )
        self.data: dict[CredentialAddress, SlotCredential] = {}
        # Writes the lock has not yet been seen to hold, by address. This is the
        # whole of "unverified": an address is verified exactly when nothing is
        # pending against it. Confirmed by a read or push showing the slot
        # present; given up on by the first read past the deadline that still
        # does not -- which is also the only way a pending write ends without
        # confirmation, so nothing outside a completed read ever has to guess.
        # Keyed by CredentialAddress, NOT by device slot: one slot can hold a
        # credential of each type, and a slot-keyed map would let two addresses
        # sharing a slot consume each other's entry.
        self._pending: dict[CredentialAddress, PendingWrite] = {}
        # Addresses whose pending write failed -- not seen by the deadline, or
        # displaced by a different code -- awaiting the sync tick's one charge
        # to the slot breaker. Consumed by ``take_failed_write``.
        self._failed_writes: set[CredentialAddress] = set()
        # The single confirmation look for this lock: a task for the immediate
        # first look, then a timer while anything stays pending. One per
        # coordinator, not per write: N pending slots on one lock are one read
        # apart, not N.
        self._confirm_task: asyncio.Task[None] | None = None
        self._confirm_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        self._lock_breaker = CircuitBreaker(
            BACKOFF_FAILURE_THRESHOLD,
            backoff_initial=timedelta(seconds=BACKOFF_INITIAL_SECONDS),
            backoff_max=timedelta(seconds=BACKOFF_MAX_SECONDS),
        )
        self._original_update_interval: timedelta | None = update_interval
        # Whether the lock has ever been reached successfully. A lock that has
        # never been reached is "not ready yet" (e.g. its integration is still
        # starting up after a Home Assistant restart), not "offline" -- so it
        # must not raise the lock_offline repair during the startup window.
        self._reached_once = False

        # Set up drift detection timer for locks with hard_refresh_interval
        if lock.hard_refresh_interval:
            self._drift_unsub = async_track_time_interval(
                hass,
                self._async_drift_check,
                lock.hard_refresh_interval,
                cancel_on_shutdown=True,
            )

        if lock.connection_check_interval:
            self._connection_unsub = async_track_time_interval(
                hass,
                self._async_connection_check,
                lock.connection_check_interval,
                cancel_on_shutdown=True,
            )

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    lock_entity_id: str,
    lock: BaseLock,
) -> bool:
    """
    Return True if another entry still holds this very lock instance.

    An entry takes a shared instance by putting it in its ``runtime_data.locks``
    and gives it up by taking it out, so whichever takes it out last tears it
    down: its push subscription, its config-entry state listener and its
    coordinator stop with no entry left to stop them otherwise. Asked by
    identity: an entry setting up while another unloads finds nothing to share

        runtime_data.locks.get(lock_entity_id) is lock

content.thinking:
I'm thinking about overriding the coordinator's refresh scheduling so it checks whether any holder has disabled polling before deferring to the default behavior, rather than relying solely on the single config entry flag.

Since the "who holds this lock" logic would need to live in domain/queries.py to avoid a circular import between the domain layer and __init__.py, I'm weighing whether to define a shared `entries_holding` predicate there and reuse it both for checking polling and for the existing "held by another entry" check—keeping the fix minimal while avoiding the kind of duplicated predicate drift I want to steer away from.

For the polling rule itself, I'm settling on: poll by default unless there's at least one holder and all holders disable polling, using zero-holder as the safe default. I'm also considering how a `pref_disable_polling` change triggers a config entry reload in HA, and that the shared coordinator might survive across that reload if another entry still holds it, with the new preference only taking effect after the next scheduled refresh fires.

I'm also reasoning that since HA's `_schedule_refresh` bails out early when polling is disabled, that applies equally to backoff retries after a failed refresh — so cold-start and backoff behavior should be exempted from assertions, and the cleanest approach is to override `_schedule_refresh` directly to match HA's exact behavior. Push-type locks with no update interval aren't affected either way, and per the Q3 decision, disabling polling should only stop the scheduled poll while drift and connection checks keep running — which matches scoping the override narrowly. I'm now thinking through a test setup using a mock config entry with polling disabled.

For the test, I'd advance time past the scan interval using the freezer and verify usercode calls don't increase, plus check the two-entries-sharing-a-lock case where polling only stops once both entries disable it. I should also fix the stale comment and the catalog row, then give the user a quick heads-up before dispatching the subagent to implement this.

input.prompt:
Fix ONE bug in the Lock Code Manager Home Assistant custom integration, as a minimal one-defect bug-fix PR branch.

WORKTREE (absolute paths only; never touch /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager itself or other worktrees): /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/shared-lock-polling
Branch: fix/shared-lock-polling-pref, created from origin/main. Commit (one commit, or a few), do NOT push. Never run bare `git stash`. Read AGENTS.md for repo conventions first.

## The bug
Since PR #1629, `LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator` (custom_components/lock_code_manager/domain/coordinator.py, ~line 121) is built with `config_entry=None`, because one lock's coordinator is shared by every Lock Code Manager config entry that holds that lock. Home Assistant's DataUpdateCoordinator honors the "Disable polling" system option (`ConfigEntry.pref_disable_polling`) by reading its own `config_entry` in `_schedule_refresh`, so with no entry the option is now ignored for every lock: a user who disabled polling still gets the lock polled every scan interval. Verify this against the installed homeassistant package's `helpers/update_coordinator.py` before relying on it.

## The approved rule (decided by the maintainer; do not relitigate)
- Poll unless EVERY entry holding the lock instance has `pref_disable_polling` set. If any holder allows polling, poll. With no holders, poll (the default).
- "Disable polling" stops ONLY the scheduled poll (what HA's own option stops). Drift checks (`hard_refresh_interval`), connection checks, the first read, push handling and confirmation reads are unaffected.
- "Holds" means the identity rule already used for teardown: an entry holds the instance when `entry.runtime_data.locks.get(lock_entity_id) is lock`, for any entry that has runtime_data, whatever its state. See `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry` in custom_components/lock_code_manager/__init__.py (~line 1043) and its docstring.

## Implementation guidance
- Add one named query for "the entries holding this lock instance" in custom_components/lock_code_manager/domain/queries.py (that module holds the named predicates about which entries manage a lock; match its style). Make `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry` use it, as a pure substitution with identical semantics, so there is exactly one definition of "holds". Do not create a circular import: domain/ must not import from the package __init__.
- In the coordinator, override `_schedule_refresh` (keep HA's signature/decorator) to return without scheduling when every holder disables polling, otherwise defer to super(). Check what HA's version does when it returns early (e.g. whether an existing unsub must be cancelled) and mirror it. Read the holders live at schedule time (don't cache), the same way HA reads its entry live.
- Update the comment at `config_entry=None` so it no longer says the option "does not apply"; state the rule (comments state intent, not history; spell out acronyms; match comment density).
- Do not touch anything else (no R2 lock-handle work, no other refactors).

## Tests (behavior level, through real setup)
Use the repo's existing integration test harness (tests/conftest.py, tests/common.py — MockLCMLock records calls; find how tests count get_usercodes reads and how they drive time with HA's `freezer` fixture; tests/providers/test_base.py has stepping helpers). Use proper setup/teardown via MockConfigEntry and hass.config_entries, not manual hass.data manipulation. Do not hand-build internal state. Cases:
1. One entry with `pref_disable_polling=True` on a polling (non-push) lock: after the first read, advancing past several scan intervals adds no scheduled reads.
2. Two entries sharing one lock, one disables and one doesn't: the lock keeps polling.
3. Two entries sharing one lock, both disable: no scheduled polls.
4. (If cheap) Polling disabled does not stop the drift/hard-refresh check, per the rule.
Each test must FAIL with the fix reverted — confirm by mutation in an rsync scratch copy under /private/tmp/claude-501/ (restore in a finally; never leave a mutant in the worktree), or by temporarily reverting and re-running, and report it.

## Verification (all must pass before committing)
- Reinstall dev requirements first if the venv may be stale (see AGENTS.md; `uv pip install -r requirements_dev.txt`).
- `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci python -m pytest tests/ -q -n auto --cov --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered` — full suite green, 100% coverage.
- `prek run --all-files` (run `yarn install` first if eslint is missing).

Commit message: `fix: honor "Disable polling" for a lock shared by several entries` with a short body (bug, rule, where), ending with:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Report: the diff summary, HA's `_schedule_refresh` behavior you mirrored, each test and whether it failed with the fix reverted, suite/coverage/prek results, commit SHA, and anything surprising.

content.thinking:
This looks like case (a) — the fix's own rule isn't being re-evaluated when the holder set changes. The minimal fix would be to trigger the coordinator's reschedule whenever an entry takes over an existing instance, but I need to think through what the cleanest mechanism for that would be.

I'm considering adding a public method like `async_holders_changed()` on the coordinator that triggers `_schedule_refresh()` when a new entry joins an existing shared instance. For leaving, I can rely on HA's existing behavior of letting an already-scheduled poll fire once harmlessly, and reloads naturally decompose into leave-then-join, so the join hook handles re-enabling too. One concern is that calling reschedule on every join could unnecessarily delay the next poll if a refresh is already pending, so I need a smarter approach than blindly rescheduling each time.

I should only trigger a reschedule if nothing is currently scheduled, checking `_unsub_refresh is None` before calling it, and naming the method consistently with existing conventions like `note_push_capability` — something like `note_holder_joined`. This gives me a concrete fix for the builder-disable test gap, and I should also add tests for the toggle flow (disable both, re-enable one via reload and confirm polling resumes) and tighten the decorative preference test by giving non-holder entries a distinct runtime_data instance to avoid false positives.

For the performance issue with push locking scanning entries on every push, a cheap fix is checking `self.update_interval is None` first before falling to super. I'll dispatch this back to the same agent since it already has the context, so I need to pull up the SendMessage tool schema.

1. DEFECT (reproduced by reviewer): the rule is only re-evaluated when something calls _schedule_refresh. An entry JOINING an existing instance (_setup_one_lock in __init__.py ~line 1840, `runtime_data.locks[lock_entity_id] = existing_lock`) never triggers it. Repro: entry A disables polling and holds lock 2; entry B allows polling, CONF_SLOTS={} (no users) and lists lock 2 -> B joins, adds no coordinator entities, nothing requests a refresh -> 0 reads over 3 scan intervals. Same gap for a slot-less entry reloaded after the user re-enables polling, and when the joiner's entities are disabled in the entity registry. It only works today because update_before_add on the joiner's slot entities incidentally requests a refresh.
   Fix: add a coordinator method following the existing `note_*` naming (e.g. `note_holder_joined`) that, unless shutdown was requested, schedules the refresh if polling is now allowed and no refresh is currently scheduled (check HA's attribute for the pending refresh handle, `_unsub_refresh`, in the installed homeassistant; don't reschedule an already-scheduled poll, which would push it a full interval later on every join). Call it where an entry takes an existing instance. Leaving needs nothing: when the last polling-allowing holder leaves, the already-scheduled poll fires once and then stops, mirroring HA's own toggle behavior; say so in a comment only if it's a trap a reader would trip on.
2. TEST: builder-disables passes only via that incidental refresh. Add a case where the joiner allows polling and has NO users (CONF_SLOTS={} or equivalent), so no entity requests a refresh; it must fail without fix 1 (confirm by mutation).
3. TEST: cover HA's real toggle flow: both holders disable polling, then re-enable it on one via hass.config_entries.async_update_entry(entry, pref_disable_polling=False) followed by a reload (as HA's websocket handler does), with the other entry keeping the shared coordinator alive -> polling resumes. Prefer the slot-less variant so it depends on fix 1. Confirm it fails without fix 1.
4. TEST: tests/test_coordinator.py ~2058, the "no holders" test: the non-holder entry has no runtime_data, so the identity check is never exercised there and the async_update_entry(pref_disable_polling=True) line is decorative. Make the non-holder entry hold a DIFFERENT instance (or a different lock) with polling disabled, so the test fails if entries_holding stops checking identity (confirm by mutation).
5. PERF: _schedule_refresh walks every entry even for push locks (update_interval None, super returns immediately) on every push update. Short-circuit: if self.update_interval is None, defer to super() before computing holders.

content.text:
Review round 1 on the polling fix found one real defect, and it was reproduced. Polling only restarts when something happens to ask for a refresh.

Here's the failing case. Entry A has polling disabled and holds a lock. Entry B allows polling, has no users, and joins that same lock. Nothing asks for a refresh, so the lock goes without a poll across three scan intervals, even though B allows it.

It currently works for an entry with users only by accident: that entry's slot entities ask for a refresh as they're added. The same gap hits a user-less entry that reloads after polling is turned back on in its settings.

The subagent is fixing it in a new commit:
- **Re-check on join:** when an entry joins a lock it now shares, it schedules a poll if polling is allowed and none is already scheduled. Rescheduling one that's already pending would push it back a full interval.
- **Test for the gap:** a joining entry with no users, which fails without the fix.
- **Test for the real toggle flow:** both entries disable polling, then one turns it back on and reloads, as Home Assistant's settings page does. Polling resumes.
- **Tighter "no holders" test:** the other entry now holds a different instance of the lock, so the "same instance" check is actually exercised.
- **Push locks skip the walk:** they now skip the entry walk that ran on every push update.

That leaves one review round. If it comes back clean, I'll open the PR so 6.0.2 can include it. The harness fixes for batch 0 are still running separately.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Home Assistant re-checks "Disable polling" only when something schedules the next refresh. Once the rule depends on which entries hold the lock, a change in who holds it also has to trigger that re-check. Otherwise the rule is correct but nothing ever asks it.
- The original tests passed through a side path: slot entities refresh as they're added. Using a joining entry with no users removes that path, so the test checks the promise itself rather than how the setup happens to behave.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**1. Joining didn't re-check the rule.**
- **Change:** I added `note_holder_joined()` to the coordinator. It returns early if shutdown was requested or a poll is already scheduled (`_unsub_refresh`, the attribute in the installed Home Assistant); otherwise it calls `_schedule_refresh()`, which applies the rule. The join branch of `_setup_one_lock` in `__init__.py` calls it after `async_wait_for_setup()`, guarded by `coordinator is not None`.
- **Leaving:** nothing is called when an entry leaves. I added no comment for it because it isn't a trap: the already-scheduled poll runs once, then stops, as with Home Assistant's own toggle.
- **Test:** `test_an_entry_joining_leaves_a_scheduled_poll_where_it_is` checks that a join doesn't push a due poll a full interval later.
- **Without the fix:** rescheduling on every join fails that test. Removing the call fails the item 2 and item 3 tests.

**2. Joiner with no users.**
- **Test:** a new case, `builder-disables-joiner-has-no-users`, in `test_a_shared_lock_is_polled_unless_every_holder_disables_polling`. The entry helper became `_entry_on_the_second_lock(None, ...)`, which builds an entry with `CONF_SLOTS={}`.
- **Without the fix:** fails.

**3. Home Assistant's toggle flow.**
- **Test:** `test_re_enabling_polling_on_one_holder_resumes_the_poll`. Both entries disable polling, and the second has no users; reads stay at 0. Then `async_update_entry(..., pref_disable_polling=False)` and `async_reload` on that entry, while the other keeps the coordinator alive; reads go to 3.
- **Without the fix:** fails.

**4. The "no holders" test now checks identity.**
- **Test:** rewritten as `test_a_lock_instance_no_entry_holds_is_polled`. A real entry with polling disabled is set up holding its own instance of lock 2. A second instance is built with `async_create_lock_instance`, and its coordinator is still polled.
- **Without the fix:** if `entries_holding` matches by entity id instead of identity, it fails.

**5. Push locks skip the holder walk.**
- **Change:** `_schedule_refresh` walks the holders only when `self.update_interval is not None`; otherwise it goes straight to `super()`.
- **Test:** none. This only saves work, so no test can see it, and removing it fails nothing.

**Verification:**
- **Full suite:** 2729 passed, 3 skipped (`HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci`, `-n auto --cov`). The integration code is at 100% coverage.
- **`prek run --all-files`:** clean. `ruff format` reformatted one test file on the first run.

**Worth knowing:**
- **Shutdown check can't be reached:** removing it fails no test. A joiner holds the instance before it waits, so no other entry can tear it down underneath it. I kept it because you asked for it.
- **No listener check:** I briefly added a "skip when the coordinator has no listeners" check to match Home Assistant, then removed it to keep to your spec. Without it, a lock whose holders have no users at all gets one poll when a polling-allowed entry joins, and Home Assistant then stops rescheduling.
- **Unrelated change left out:** `.entire/.gitignore` has a change I didn't make (`redactors/local/`), probably from a tool. I didn't commit it, and it is still unstaged.</result>

input.message:
Round 2 (final) review on 47e0c455 found defects in the round-1 fixes. Fix them in ONE new commit on top (no amend, no push), same worktree /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/regression-harness, same verification (full suite -n auto --cov, 100% on custom_components; test_harness.py 3x; prek), mutations only in a /private/tmp/claude-501/ scratch copy restored in finally. Keep the change narrow: this is the last round, so no new features.

1. DOUBLE TICK (reproduced by reviewer). The per-timer stepping in async_advance_sync_ticks fires a sync manager's 2 s interval tick TWICE in one call when it is overdue or due within CLOCK_STEP of the start: it fires early in the span, HA re-arms it at fire-time + 2 s, which is still < end = start + TICK_INTERVAL + CLOCK_STEP. Repro: after one advance, freezer.tick(1.996) or freezer.tick(1.9995), then async_advance_sync_ticks -> each of the 4 _TrackTimeInterval(2s) timers fires 2x. Also the offset drifts down by CLOCK_STEP per call with no clock movement, so call #666 of a plain loop double-ticks. That breaks "fires once" / "each failure on a tick of its own" and makes async_tick_until counts and async_trip_slot_breaker's MAX_SYNC_ATTEMPTS budget wrong.
   Required invariant: each call fires every sync manager's interval tick EXACTLY once, whatever the starting phase, while still firing other timers in due-time order. Suggested mechanism (your call if you find better): bound the stepping by the sync tick timers' own due times — identify the scheduled sync interval handles, and step through timers in order up to the LATEST of those due times (plus the microsecond landing margin) instead of to start + TICK_INTERVAL + CLOCK_STEP. Since all sync ticks are due within one interval of now, each fires once and its re-arm lands past the bound. Fail loudly if no sync tick timer is scheduled (instead of silently advancing). Make sure the existing "the scheduled tick really runs" tests and the +0.5 s timer-ordering test still pass.
   Add a harness test that pins exactly-one-tick-per-call: count firings of the sync interval tick across calls started at awkward phases (overdue, due within CLOCK_STEP, due exactly at end, freezer.tick(1.996), freezer.tick(1.9995)) and across many consecutive calls (enough to cross the old drift point cheaply — e.g. simulate the drift with freezer ticks rather than 666 calls). It must fail on 47e0c455's implementation.
2. clear_faults now iterates the module-level _INSTALLED_FAULTS set (hash order), releasing held calls in arbitrary order (reviewer saw [10, 8, 5, 6, 9, 7] for slots 5..10, 50/50 trials). Release this lock's faults in install order (keep a per-lock ordered record that includes spent faults, or an insertion-ordered dict for _INSTALLED_FAULTS). Add a test asserting release order for several held writes.
3. Off-by-one in the for/else 1000-timer cap: the `now >= end` check runs only at the top of each iteration, so reaching the end on exactly the 1000th jump still falls into `else` and fails. Fix the loop so completing on the last allowed jump succeeds. (If fix 1 restructures the loop, just make sure the cap is right.)
4. The trailing release_all_faults() in the pytest_runtest_teardown wrapper's finally runs after all fixture finalizers, including the event loop close, so setting an Event a call still waits on can raise "Event loop is closed". After teardown, only DISCARD leftover faults (empty _INSTALLED_FAULTS) without touching events/futures; keep the release BEFORE fixture teardown. Update the hook test accordingly.
5. test_teardown_releases_faults_before_the_fixtures_and_after drives the hook generator by hand, so it doesn't prove pytest orders it before fixture finalizers. Keep it if useful, but make sure the real-ordering test (test_a_write_left_held_does_not_hang_teardown or similar) would fail if tryfirst were removed or the release moved after teardown — confirm by mutation; if that's not achievable reliably, say so.

Commit message: `test: fire each sync tick once per advance; release faults in order` + short body + trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Report per item: change, test, fail-before confirmation (including the reviewer's repro phases for item 1), suite/coverage/prek, SHA.

There's also a subtler edge case where joining during an in-flight poll could leave an extra timer if the finally block skips rescheduling, though the listener check narrows that risk.

For the shutdown guard, I'm trying to recall whether HA's actual `_schedule_refresh` implementation checks for a shutdown state before scheduling — I don't believe it does, which suggests this guard path may be unreachable in practice. Since it's both untested and likely unreachable, I'm leaning toward dropping it rather than adding a test for dead code.

For the remaining items, I'm deciding to skip the polling-disable toggle edge case as out of scope, and drop the push short-circuit optimization too since the entry count is small enough that the perf gain is negligible and the agent flagged it as untestable.

So I'll land three narrow fixes: add the listeners check, drop the shutdown guard, and drop the push short-circuit, each verified by a tiny targeted test. Given this is already round 3, I'll stop here rather than iterate further, note the private-attribute dependencies and accepted edge cases in the PR body as known limitations, and send this over to the polling agent.

I'll fix the three small issues found in round 2 (require listeners before scheduling a poll, remove the unreachable shutdown guard, and drop the no-op push-lock shortcut), while documenting the two accepted edge cases (join-during-poll and stuck-entry) in the PR body instead of fixing them.

content.text:
Both branches have had their two review rounds. Their last fixes are being made now, each kept narrow and checked against the reviewer's own reproductions:

**Polling fix (`fix/shared-lock-polling-pref`):** the changes are adding the listener check and deleting the two guards. After that it goes up as a one-defect PR for 6.0.2, using the template and linked to this thread.

**Batch 0 harness (`test/regression-harness`):** the fixes are:
- each call fires every sync tick exactly once, whatever the clock phase it starts at;
- `clear_faults` releases held calls in the order they were installed;
- the off-by-one in the timer limit;
- after teardown, leftover faults are only discarded, so nothing touches a closed event loop.

A new test pins "one tick per call" at the starting phases the reviewer found awkward.

Neither gets a third open review round, which is the cap we set. If either agent's report shows the fix spreading beyond what was asked, I'll stop and bring it to you instead of patching again.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The double tick is a classic trap when simulating time. Moving the clock to "start + 2 s" assumes the next tick is a full interval away, but a repeating timer re-arms from when it last fired. If it fired early in the window, its next run also falls inside the window. Bounding each step by the ticks' own due times keeps the count right whatever the phase.
- On the polling side, both round-2 fixes delete code. A guard no test can reach, or a shortcut the parent class already takes, adds lines without adding behavior. A mutation that survives with the whole suite green is how you spot that.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

- Raman asked whether to revert merged bug-fix PRs #1623–#1634 before a possible core rebuild. Answer: no. Provider fixes (#1624/#1625/#1627) survive any rebuild; core fixes (#1623/#1629/#1632/#1633) become the rebuilt core's spec via behavior-level regression tests (batch 1); #1634 is behavior-neutral. Only exception: #1629 regressed "Disable polling" (shared coordinator has config_entry=None, so HA's _schedule_refresh check never fires). Fixed on fix/shared-lock-polling-pref before publishing draft 6.0.2, per approved decision 2: poll unless every entry holding the lock instance (identity: runtime_data.locks.get(id) is lock) disables polling; no holders → poll; only scheduled poll stops.
- Fix shape: domain/queries.py entries_holding() (also used by _lock_instance_held_by_another_entry), coordinator _schedule_refresh override, note_holder_joined() called when an entry joins an existing instance (schedules only if allowed, none scheduled, and listeners exist). Accepted edges: join during in-flight poll may leave one extra poll; FAILED_UNLOAD holder re-enabling polling without reload doesn't restart.
- Regression harness (test/regression-harness) lesson: stepping a frozen clock from start to start+interval can fire a repeating interval timer twice if it was due early in the window (it re-arms at fire+interval). Bound the step by the repeating timers' own due times.
- New catalog bugs: writes failing as disconnected while reads succeed never suspend (reads reset the lock breaker) — open; a refused write doesn't update _last_operation_time so isn't paced — unverified.

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/pr-polling-body.md <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

Since #1629, every lock's coordinator is built with `config_entry=None`, because one lock's coordinator is shared by every Lock Code Manager entry that holds that lock. Home Assistant applies the "Disable polling" system option inside `DataUpdateCoordinator._schedule_refresh`, by reading the coordinator's own config entry. With no entry, the option was ignored for every lock: a lock kept being polled every scan interval even after the user disabled polling.

This restores the option for shared locks with one rule: **a lock is polled unless every entry holding it disables polling.** If any holder allows polling, the lock is polled. A lock no entry holds is polled too. As with Home Assistant's own option, only the scheduled poll stops. Drift checks, connection checks, the first read, push updates and confirmation reads keep running.

- **`domain/queries.py`:** new `entries_holding`, every entry holding one lock instance in any state, matched by identity. `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry` (release) now uses it, so "holds" has one definition. It covers the same entries as before.
- **`domain/coordinator.py`:** `_schedule_refresh` reads the holders each time it schedules. `note_holder_joined` re-checks the rule when another entry takes the instance. Without it, nothing would restart polling when an entry that allows it joins a lock every other holder had stopped polling. It schedules only if the rule allows a poll, none is already scheduled, and something listens. That matches Home Assistant, and a join never pushes a due poll a full interval later.
- **`__init__.py`:** the join branch of lock setup calls `note_holder_joined`.

Tests go through real setup with `MockConfigEntry`, the `freezer` fixture and `MockLCMLock` read counts:
- polling disabled stops the scheduled poll;
- the drift check keeps running;
- a shared lock in each combination (one holder disables, both disable, the joiner has no users);
- Home Assistant's toggle flow: `async_update_entry`, then reload, resumes polling;
- a join leaves an already-scheduled poll where it is;
- a lock nothing listens to isn't polled;
- an instance no entry holds is polled.

Every test that checks polling stops fails when the fix is reverted. The tests that check polling continues catch a rule that is too strict (`any` instead of `all`, or checking only one holder), and mutation confirms that.

**Accepted edge cases:**
- **Join during an in-flight poll:** an entry joining while a scheduled poll is running can leave one extra poll behind, if that poll's own reschedule is then skipped (Home Assistant stopping, or listeners removed at the same moment).
- **Entry stuck in FAILED_UNLOAD:** turning polling back on for that entry doesn't restart polling until something else reschedules. Home Assistant only reloads loaded entries on a preference change, and an entry stuck in FAILED_UNLOAD already holds its instance by design.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes a regression from #1629, unreleased (draft 6.0.2)
- This PR is related to issue: #1629

I've opened the polling fix as **#1635** and linked it to this thread. It's ready for your review, and 6.0.2 can ship once it merges.

**The bug:** since #1629, a lock that several entries share has ignored the "Disable polling" setting. That change hasn't been released yet; it's in the draft 6.0.2.

**The fix** follows your rule: a lock is polled unless every entry holding it disables polling.
- It covers only the regular scheduled poll. Drift checks, connection checks, the first read and push updates keep running.
- When another entry starts sharing a lock, the rule is checked again, so a newly added entry that allows polling turns it back on.

**Testing:**
- The full suite passes with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean.
- Every test that checks polling stops also fails with the fix removed.
- Review hit the two-round cap. Round 1 found the real gap: polling never restarted when a new entry that allows it started sharing the lock. Round 2 found three small issues, two of which were fixed by deleting code.

The PR body names two rare edge cases we're accepting rather than fixing:
- An entry that starts sharing a lock while a poll is running can leave one extra poll behind.
- Turning polling back on for an entry stuck in "failed to unload" doesn't restart polling.

I also marked the regression in the catalog as fixed by #1635.

**Batch 0 harness:** the round-2 fixes are still running: one sync tick per call, faults released in the order they were set, the off-by-one, and cleanup that never touches a closed event loop. Once they come back and check out, I'll open the test-only PR the same way.

It counts interval firings per manager by recording `_async_tick` calls that get a timestamp; the first tick a manager runs at start gets none and isn't counted. It checks one aligning call, then a phase move, then 6 back-to-back calls. The phases are: overdue, due as the call starts, due within 0.5 ms, due one clock step in, the reviewer's `freezer.tick(1.996)` and `freezer.tick(1.9995)`, and no time between calls.

- **Existing tests:** the scheduled-tick tests and the +0.5 s timer-ordering test still pass.
- **Tests that now need a loaded entry:** three clock tests. The two-clocks test now asserts both clocks moved the same amount and by more than 2 intervals across 3 calls, not at least 3 intervals. Each call now only moves to the next tick, so a call after the first moves slightly under 2 s.
- **New test:** `test_advancing_sync_ticks_fails_with_no_sync_tick_scheduled`. Reverting the check makes it fail.

- **Change:** `_INSTALLED_FAULTS` is now a dict, which keeps install order. `clear_faults` and `release_all_faults` release in that order.
- **Test:** `test_clear_faults_releases_held_calls_in_install_order` holds 20 writes and checks they answer in install order.
- **Fail-before:** going back to set order fails it, 5 out of 5 runs.

**3. Off-by-one in the 1000-jump cap.**
- **Change:** the stepping is now `_async_step_timers_to`. It always jumps at least once (so an overdue timer fires), and checks whether it has reached the end after each jump, so finishing on the last allowed jump succeeds.
- **Test:** `test_stepping_may_reach_the_end_on_its_last_allowed_jump` sets the cap to 1.
- **Fail-before:** the old check-at-the-top loop fails it.

**4. Release after the loop closes.**
- **Change:** the teardown hook still releases everything before fixture teardown. Afterwards it only calls the new `forget_all_faults()`, which empties the registry without setting any event.
- **Test:** the hook test now has a late fault holding a call while the hook finishes. It asserts the call is still held, and that `clear_faults` no longer sees the fault, then releases it by hand.
- **Fail-before:** putting `release_all_faults()` back in the `finally` fails it.

- **Release moved after teardown:** `test_a_write_left_held_does_not_hang_teardown` catches this. Its teardown hangs until pytest-timeout (60 s) errors it, so it is caught as a hang, not as a quick failure.

If sync managers have different phases (for example, one restarted after a reload) and settling takes longer than the gap between their due times, the earliest manager's next tick could fire inside the settle. With test operation delays at 0, settling normally takes a few milliseconds, and no current test hits this.</result>

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/pr-harness-body.md <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

This is batch 0 of a regression-test net. Every reported bug should get a test through Lock Code Manager's user-facing surfaces (entity states, actions, repairs, flows, events) before the domain core is reworked. This PR only builds the harness those tests need. It adds no bug tests and changes no production code.

**Clock helpers** for Home Assistant's `freezer` fixture, which moves both `time.monotonic` and the event loop's clock. The helpers are shared in `tests/common.py`, moved out of `tests/providers/test_base.py` (#1628):
- `async_step_clock_until`
- `async_run_paced`
- `async_settle_background`
- `async_run_until_quiet`

**Time-driven sync tick:**
- **`async_advance_sync_ticks`** runs the real scheduled sync tick by moving the clock. It doesn't call sync internals. - `held` (calls held right now);
- a bounded `async_wait_held()`;
- `clear()`;

Both PRs are open, linked to this thread, and ready for your review:

- **#1635:** the fix for "Disable polling" being ignored on locks shared by several entries. This came from #1629. It should merge before 6.0.2 is published.
- **#1636:** batch 0 of the regression net. It's the test harness only; there's no production code in it.

**About #1636:**
- **What it adds:**
  - a sync-tick helper that moves the clock to run the real scheduled tick;
  - helpers that run ticks until a condition holds, or until a slot's breaker trips;
  - five fault knobs on the mock lock (ignore, refuse, fail, hang, drop reply);
  - teardown that can't hang on a held call.
- **Results:** the full suite passes (2773 tests) with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean. The harness's own 53 tests run in about 3 s, and each review fix has a test that failed before it.
- **Reviews:** it took the two allowed rounds. Round 2 caught a bug my round-1 fix had introduced: one helper call could fire a sync tick twice. The fix and a test pinning "exactly one tick per call" are in.
- **Known limit, written up in the PR body:** if two sync managers tick at very different times, one could tick again while background work is settling. No current test runs into this.

Once #1636 merges, batch 1 starts. It converts about 14 bugs whose tests check internals into tests on what users see: entity states, actions and repairs.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The harness PR changed shape across the two review rounds, but every finding was in test code that the branch itself had introduced. That's the case where fixing in place is right. Backing out applies when fixes start touching the design itself.
- One finding couldn't be pinned down: `tryfirst` on the teardown hook. pytest runs any wrapper's code before its `yield` ahead of the built-in fixture teardown anyway, so `tryfirst` only matters once a second wrapper exists. When a mutation survives, check whether the guard has any effect today before writing a test for it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

### Findings worth raising separately

- **#1536 is only partly fixed.** The user subentry flow's `several` / `one` / `reconfigure` steps still wait on the allocation read with no progress step. Probe-confirmed. Row F "#1536 (residual)".

- **The Akuvox/virtual "ignored clear" loop is real on main.** 30 clears in 30 ticks, with no charge and no repair. It is the polled-lock twin of #1622. Row D.

- **Two roadmap review items are not present on main:**

### Found by batch 0 (2026-10-11), open

- **Writes fail as disconnected while reads succeed, so the slot never suspends.** Each successful read resets the lock breaker, and the slot retries every 2 s forever. This is the "retry path must match failure mode" class. Add a strict xfail in batch 11 (seam, `MockLCMLock.fail(None, error=LockDisconnected)` on writes only).

- **(Unverified) A refused write doesn't count toward pacing.** `BaseLock` updates `_last_operation_time` only after a call succeeds, so the next operation after a refusal is not paced. A refusal is still a round trip to the device. Check during batch 2 (pacing, #139/PR #760) whether this can hammer a lock that keeps refusing; the strict xfail goes in batch 11 if it can.

input.description: Batch 1: convert I-only bug tests to B
input.prompt:
You are writing batch 1 of a regression-test net for the Lock Code Manager Home Assistant custom integration. TEST-ONLY PR: no production code changes (custom_components/ untouched). If you find a real bug, STOP that item and report it; do not fix it.

WORKTREE (absolute paths only; never touch /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager itself or other worktrees): /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/regression-batch1
Branch: test/regression-batch1 from origin/main (f4f49e57). Commit (one or a few commits), do NOT push. Never run bare `git stash`. Read AGENTS.md first (it documents the harness). Create a venv in the worktree if needed (`uv venv --python 3.14 && uv pip install -r requirements_dev.txt`; .venv is gitignored); `yarn install` if prek's eslint needs it.

## Why
The domain core (coordinator, sync tick, pending writes, breakers, lock ownership) may be rebuilt. Every fixed bug needs a guard that survives that rebuild. These 13 bugs are guarded today only by "I-level" tests: tests that assert on or drive core internals (`coordinator.data`, `coordinator._pending`, breaker fields like `_slot_breaker.failure_count`, `SlotSyncManager` private state, `async_trigger_sync_tick` which forces manager state and calls `_async_tick`, private provider methods like `_pin_state`, `runtime_data.locks` identity, spies on `async_shutdown`, `_setup_succeeded`, `_push_unsubs`). A rebuild breaks or blinds those.

## The rule for every new test ("B level")
- Drive ONLY through Home Assistant surfaces or the library-level fakes: real config entries set up via hass.config_entries, entity states (in-sync binary sensor, code sensors, active/enabled entities), repairs (issue registry, e.g. `slot_suspended`), events, services/actions, the provider e2e harnesses' fake nodes/clients and their recorded calls, `MockLCMLock`'s recorded `service_calls`.
- Time moves ONLY via the batch 0 harness in tests/common.py: `async_advance_sync_ticks(hass, freezer, ...)`, `async_tick_until(hass, freezer, done, max_ticks=..., what=...)`, `async_trip_slot_breaker`, plus fault knobs on MockLCMLock (`ignore/refuse/fail/hang/drop_reply`) and the clock helpers. Never `async_trigger_sync_tick`. Read tests/test_harness.py for usage.
- Assert NOTHING internal. No `coordinator.data`, no private attributes, no patches of `domain.*`.
- Tests must not build their own input contract: feed the scenario the way the real lock/library would (fake node value updates / notifications, MQTT payloads, fake client responses), not hand-built LCM-internal objects.
- ADD the B test next to the existing I test; do NOT delete or rewrite the I tests (they go when the core is swapped).
- Each new test MUST FAIL with its fix reverted. Prove it per test: in an rsync scratch copy under /private/tmp/claude-501/ (restore in a `finally`, never leave a mutant in the worktree), revert or disable the fix (the PR's diff via `gh pr diff <n>` / `git log -S`, or the narrowest mutation of the guarding logic when the fix is old and spread) and show the new test fails. If you cannot make the test fail on reverting the fix, the test is not a guard — say so and keep working on it, or report it as not convertible with the reason.

## The 13 bugs (catalog rows: bug | scenario | current I guard | suggested B guard)
1. PR #819 / PR #1625 — cleared slot reads `****` or the old code and is re-cleared on every report. UC lock reports Available + masked/leftover code; no PIN wanted. I: tests/providers/zwave_js/test_e2e.py::TestUserCodeReports::test_an_available_slot_no_pin_is_wanted_on_is_empty (asserts coordinator.data). B: same e2e, assert code sensor / in-sync entity and count deletes on the fake node.
2. PR #863 — wanted PIN rewritten forever after a stale Available (lock sends Available ~3 s after a set; zwave_js). I: TestUserCodeReports::test_a_stale_available_does_not_empty_a_wanted_slot (coordinator.data; async_trigger_sync_tick). NOTE: its `[masked]` parametrization pins a KNOWN OPEN bug (#863 vs #819); do not convert that case, only the non-masked one. B: tick with freezer helpers; in-sync `on`, no rewrite (count sets on the fake node).
3. PR #1623 — second entry's slot emptied on a stale Available (shared lock, slot owned by non-creating entry). I: test_e2e.py::TestSharedLock::test_a_stale_available_on_the_second_entrys_slot_keeps_its_code; tests/test_sensor.py::test_sensor_unreadable_code_on_a_shared_lock_shows_its_entrys_pin. B: tick via time; assert in-sync / code entities (variants where the creator is disabled/failed/reloading if cheap).
4. PR #1327 — keypad/UI/service changes never reach LCM (locks routed to User Code emit no unified events). I: TestUserCodeReports::test_an_enabled_slot_reads_its_code_field. B: a keypad change reported by the fake node turns in-sync `off` (and sync then restores it if that's the behavior).
5. #1321 / PR #1322 — all entities unavailable after boot until manual reload (zwave_js entry not LOADED when LCM sets up). I: test_e2e.py::TestColdStartRace::test_lcm_setup_survives_zwave_entry_not_loaded (asserts _setup_succeeded, _push_unsubs). B: same scenario; entities unavailable before and available after zwave loads; a report then reaches in-sync.
6. #776 / PR #786 — endless set loop; code alternates PIN / `****` (masked-PIN lock, Schlage BE469; zwave_js). I: tests/providers/zwave_js/test_events.py::test_uc_shim_masked_code_pushes_unreadable; test_provider.py::test_pin_state_projects_masked_codes_as_unreadable. B: zwave_js e2e: set a slot, then a UC report Enabled + `****`; over several ticks in-sync stays `on` and the set is sent once.
7. PR #1471 (stale Available, zwave-js-ui) — synced slot unwound by a stale Available push (`userIdStatus=0` on a slot expecting a PIN). I: tests/providers/zwave_js_ui/test_e2e.py::TestPushUpdates::test_stale_available_does_not_unwind_a_synced_slot (coordinator.data). B: in-sync entity stays on, no extra `set` sendCommand.
8. PR #1624 — refused (Supervision Fail) write shown as written (zwave-js-ui returns {"status": 2}). I: tests/providers/zwave_js_ui/test_e2e.py::TestRefusedSet::test_a_supervision_fail_leaves_the_slot_out_of_sync (uses _slot_breaker). B: replace the breaker-field assertion with the `slot_suspended` repair appearing after the threshold of refused writes, in-sync `off`.
9. PR #1629 — shared lock stops polling/confirming after its creator is disabled/reloaded. I: tests/providers/zwave_js/test_e2e.py::TestSharedCoordinatorLifetime (3 tests); tests/test_init.py::test_a_shared_polled_lock_keeps_polling_after_the_entry_that_built_it_leaves (coordinator.data, spies async_shutdown). B: seam: disable the creator entry through hass.config_entries, advance past the scan interval; MockLCMLock's recorded get_usercodes calls grow; the second entry's entities see an external change.
10. #358 — in-sync and code sensors unavailable; endless "out of sync" (entity wrote state before being added). I: tests/test_binary_sensor.py::test_startup_no_code_flapping_when_synced (tick helper). B: seam: after setup, in-sync is on/off (not unavailable), using time advance.
11. #101 (+#405 item 3, PRs #126/#248/#532) — every start clears then re-sets codes already on the lock. Current: tests/providers/zha/test_e2e.py::TestSync::test_codes_already_on_the_lock_are_not_rewritten (B partial); tests/test_binary_sensor.py::test_startup_no_code_flapping_when_synced (I). B gaps: assert ZERO clears (and zero sets) for codes already on the lock; add an unload-then-setup restart case.
12. PR #737 — code changed at the lock never rewritten (external change via poll/push/drift). Current B covers poll/push; the drift path is only via `_async_drift_check` (I). B: a lock with a hard_refresh_interval; change the code out of band on the fake so only the drift check can see it; advance time past hard_refresh_interval with freezer; in-sync goes off then the code is rewritten.
13. PR #1437 — disabled slot cleared every tick forever (lock withholds codes; inactive slot). I: tests/test_binary_sensor.py::test_a_lock_that_withholds_its_contents_is_cleared_once; ::test_a_set_that_lands_but_raises_still_invalidates_the_clear (tick helper, last_write_was_clear). B: same scenarios with time-driven ticks, counting clears at the seam (MockLCMLock service_calls), cleared once over several ticks.

Put each new test next to its I counterpart (same file/class where the harness lives), named for the behavior, with a one-line docstring naming the bug (e.g. "Regression for #1437: ..."). Match the surrounding code's style, comment density and naming. Comments state intent, not history; spell out acronyms; no Google-style Args/Returns; no inline imports; no nonlocal/global; prefer comprehensions/next(). Minimize caplog text assertions.

If an item needs a harness capability that doesn't exist (e.g. the zwave_js fake node can't express a scenario), do the smallest test-only harness addition in tests/ and say so; if it's large, skip the item and report what's missing.

## Verification (all must pass before committing)
- `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci python -m pytest tests/ -q -n auto --cov --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered`: full suite green, 100% coverage on custom_components.
- Run the new tests 3 times to check for flakiness; they must be fast (the whole suite runs in well under a minute).
- `prek run --all-files`.
Commit message(s) like `test: guard <area> regressions through entity state` with a short body listing bugs covered, ending with the trailer:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

## Report
A table: bug | new test (file::name) | what it asserts | fail-with-fix-reverted evidence (what you reverted, how it failed) | notes. Then: items not converted and why, any real bugs found (with reproduction), harness additions, suite/coverage/prek results, commit SHAs.

**Batch 1** (`test/regression-batch1`, worktree `.worktrees/regression-batch1`) is underway. A subagent is adding a user-facing test next to each of 13 bugs that are currently guarded only by tests on internals:
- **Z-Wave JS:** #819/#1625, #863, #1327, #1321, #776.
- **Z-Wave JS UI:** #1471's stale Available, #1624.
- **Shared locks:** #1623, #1629.
- **Startup and sync:** #358, #101, #737's drift path, #1437.

The ground rules for each new test:
- **What it may touch:** it uses only real setup, entity states, repairs and the fake device's recorded calls.
- **How time moves:** only through batch 0's time-driven tick.
- **Must fail without the fix:** each test has to fail when its fix is reverted, checked in a scratch copy.
- **Old tests stay:** the existing internal tests remain until the core is swapped.
- **Bugs aren't fixed here:** if it finds a real bug, it stops on that item and reports it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "Must fail with the fix reverted" is the test of whether a guard is real. A new test that passes either way is just describing the code.
- Keeping the internal tests alongside the new ones is deliberate. For now both sets agree. When the core is swapped, the internal ones break, and the user-facing ones are what tell us the new core still behaves.

Result:
I reviewed commit 992da80d against origin/main and found six problems; the four biggest are below. I didn't modify the worktree. To check that each new test fails when its fix is removed, I put small code changes into a scratch copy, one at a time, and ran the tests against each.

**Tests that do fail without their fix:** #819, #863 (leftover-code case), #776, #1327, #1321, both #1623 tests, #1629 (Z-Wave JS and `test_init`), #1624, #1471, #737, and both #1437 tests. None of the new tests pins the open #863 masked case as correct. One older test, `test_a_stale_available_does_not_empty_a_wanted_slot[masked]`, does expect `known("****")`, which is that open bug. It is already on main, so it is not one of the findings.

**The `unfinished_tasks` change:** it skips only tracked tasks whose name ends in `_client_listen`. Lock Code Manager never names a task that way, so it cannot hide a task Lock Code Manager leaks. The future handling only avoids calling `get_name()` on executor futures; they are still waited on.

**Main problems:**
- **#863 and #1623 tests rely on a report the driver never sends.** They send `userIdStatus=Available` on its own. In the node-zwave-js source, every path writes the status and the code together, and an event fires even when a value is unchanged. When I sent a real paired report after a set, with the code field empty, `"0000"` or `"****"`, the slot was written again. Only a code field that still holds the PIN avoids the rewrite.
- **The `_UserCodeLock` fake doesn't match the driver.** Its writes never send the "credential added/modified/deleted" events the driver sends after a successful write. Its clear reports the leftover code instead of the empty one the driver records.
- **The #776 test only passes because masking is switched on mid-test.** When the fake masks from the start, the test fails on an extra write to slot 1.
- **The #101 test doesn't detect its fix being removed.** I removed the sync's wait for the slot's state to load and both cases still passed; only a unit test in `tests/test_sync.py` caught it.

content.thinking:
I'm realizing this matches the actual #863 scenario: node-zwave-js always pairs status with code, so a genuine stale Available report (status + empty/zero code) arriving ~3 seconds after a set is what causes the sync logic to incorrectly rewrite the wanted PIN.

That rewrite happens once per occurrence, not forever, so whether this still counts as the original #863 bug is unclear—if the lock genuinely can't be distinguished from a real deletion, LCM may be unable to tell stale Available apart from an actual code removal, which is really the #863-vs-#819 decision problem rather than a straightforward test-input bug.

So for the batch, I'm thinking the #863/#1623 tests should use the Available-plus-leftover-PIN input form, since that's what the fix actually addresses, while flagging the Available-plus-empty-code scenario as the still-open design question for later. I also need to decide what events the fake user-code lock should emit on write and delete so they match what the driver actually fires, including whether delete should produce Available plus an empty string to mirror the real clearCachedUserCodes behavior.

For #819, since the lock reports Available plus a masked/leftover code after a clear via a separate subsequent report rather than the driver's own cache-clear event, I think the fake's delete should emit the driver-correct Available-plus-empty, with the masked report sent afterward as its own node report. I also need to fix the KeyError when clearing an already-empty slot, and for #776 I'm reasoning that a masked lock from startup should trigger exactly one write attempt per slot since it can never be verified — so the test needs correcting to expect a single write rather than looping.

content.text:
Batch 1 is back with the subagent to fix what the first review round found. It hasn't been pushed, and this is round 1 of the two-round limit.

The first draft added a user-facing test for 12 of the 13 bugs, each proven to fail when its fix is removed. The 13th, #358, has no fix left in the code to remove, so the #101 test checks its symptom instead. The review found six problems:

1. **Input the driver never sends (#863, #1623):** these tests send an "Available" status on its own. The reviewer read node-zwave-js and found the driver always reports status and code together. Sent the real paired report, LCM wrote the slot again. The subagent will first check that claim itself against the driver source, tracing through the server and client libraries to HA's Z-Wave JS integration.
   - Then it measures how LCM handles each possible paired code: the leftover PIN, empty, `0000` and `****`.
   - If LCM writes a bounded number of times and then settles, that guards the bug as reported ("rewritten forever").
   - If it loops, that's a real bug, and the subagent will stop and report it rather than fix it.
   - Whether an "Available" paired with an empty code should be trusted is still the open "#863 vs #819" question, so no test will settle it either way.
2. **The fake Z-Wave lock doesn't behave like the driver.** It skips the credential events the driver sends after a successful write. It reports the old code after a clear, where the driver records an empty slot. It raises an error on clearing an empty slot, where the driver succeeds.
3. **#776 turns masking on halfway through the test.** A real masking lock masks from the start. The test will instead check that each masked slot is written at most once and never again.
4. **#101 never reaches the startup window its fix covers.** If no setup driven through real entities can reach it, I'll report #101 as only partly converted.
5. **A harness helper skips tasks by name.** It will skip only the specific Z-Wave JS listen task instead.

The subagent also raised a design question, which I've added to the catalog to bring to you before the core rebuild. If a slot's condition entity doesn't exist yet when sync starts, the slot is treated as inactive. It gets cleared, then set again once the entity appears. That's #101's symptom, but it only happens when the condition's integration loads after Home Assistant finishes starting. Should a missing condition entity mean "not ready yet" instead?

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The main finding is the "tests must not build their own input contract" lesson coming back. A hand-written report the driver can't produce shows that LCM handles a made-up input, not that the bug is guarded. Checking the input against the driver source is part of writing the test.
- The open "#863 vs #819" question shows up again here. Batch 1 can guard what was actually reported (an endless rewrite) without deciding which "Available" reports to trust. That keeps a test-only PR from quietly making a design call.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
